PETITION FOR DISSOLUTION OF MARRIAGE (DIVORCE) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Petition for Dissolution of Marriage — Information Sheet concerns the marriage of Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee, who were married on June 12, 2015. It is prepared for use alongside an actual petition for dissolution of marriage that would be filed in the California superior court for Sacramento County. This information sheet describes California's statutory dissolution process — the filing and residency requirements, the legal grounds, and the waiting period before a judgment becomes final — as background for that filing. It is not itself a court filing, and completing it does not dissolve, terminate, or otherwise change the marital status of Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee. Only a court judgment of dissolution can do that.

DISSOLUTION, LEGAL SEPARATION, AND NULLITY ARE THREE DISTINCT PROCEEDINGS
California law addresses the end or alteration of a marriage's legal status through three legally distinct types of proceeding, grouped within the same division of the Family Code but governed by different statutory parts: dissolution of marriage, legal separation of the parties, and nullity of marriage. A proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties is commenced by filing a petition that must itself state which of the two is sought. Nullity — a judicial determination that a marriage was void or voidable from the start — is governed by an entirely separate part of the same division, with its own distinct grounds (for example, that a party was under 18 at the time of the marriage without the statutory exception applying) that are unrelated to the no-fault dissolution grounds described elsewhere in this document. This document addresses only the dissolution and legal-separation process; it does not address nullity, and does not itself determine which of the three proceedings applies to any specific marriage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties is commenced by filing a petition or joint petition entitled “In re the marriage of ____ and ____,” which shall state whether it is a petition for dissolution of the marriage or for legal separation of the parties."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2330(a) (California Legislative Information text), a dissolution/legal-separation petition must state which is sought (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2330.)
  "A marriage is voidable and may be adjudged a nullity if any of the following conditions existed at the time of the marriage: (a) The party who commences the proceeding or on whose behalf the proceeding is commenced was under 18 years of age, unless the party entered into the marriage pursuant to Section 302 or 303."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2210 (California Legislative Information text), nullity's distinct, separately codified grounds (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2210.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's dissolution-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or divorce. This document is informational: it does not itself dissolve a marriage, establish residency, or determine grounds for any specific case; only a court judgment does that. These two citations are to two different Family Code sections (§ 2330 and § 2210), not subsections of the same section. This document does not describe nullity's substantive grounds in full, or the separate 'void marriage' category (incestuous and bigamous marriages, addressed in a different chapter this document's research did not independently re-verify with a second fetch); it cites § 2210's voidable-marriage grounds only as evidence that nullity is governed by a distinct statutory framework from dissolution, not as a complete statement of nullity law.

LEGAL GROUNDS FOR DISSOLUTION: A NO-FAULT STANDARD
Dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties in California may be based on only two grounds, pleaded generally rather than by reciting the underlying facts: irreconcilable differences that have caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage, or permanent legal incapacity to make decisions. Irreconcilable differences are grounds the court determines to be substantial reasons for not continuing the marriage and that make it appear the marriage should be dissolved. A marriage may be dissolved on the ground of permanent legal incapacity to make decisions only upon proof, including competent medical or psychiatric testimony, that the spouse was, at the time the petition was filed, and remains, permanently lacking the legal capacity to make decisions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Dissolution of the marriage or legal separation of the parties may be based on either of the following grounds, which shall be pleaded generally: (a) Irreconcilable differences, which have caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage. (b) Permanent legal incapacity to make decisions."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2310(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the two exclusive, generally-pleaded grounds for dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2310.)
  "Irreconcilable differences are those grounds which are determined by the court to be substantial reasons for not continuing the marriage and which make it appear that the marriage should be dissolved."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2311 (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definition of irreconcilable differences (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2311.)
  "A marriage may be dissolved on the grounds of permanent legal incapacity to make decisions only upon proof, including competent medical or psychiatric testimony, that the spouse was at the time the petition was filed, and remains, permanently lacking the legal capacity to make decisions."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2312 (California Legislative Information text), the proof standard for permanent legal incapacity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2312.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's dissolution-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or divorce. This document is informational: it does not itself dissolve a marriage, establish residency, or determine grounds for any specific case; only a court judgment does that. This clause verifies that California Family Code § 2310 lists exactly two grounds and requires that they be "pleaded generally"; the statement that California's dissolution statute contains no fault-based ground (such as adultery or cruelty) is drawn from the absence of any such ground in § 2310's text, not from a separate statute that affirmatively abolishes fault grounds — no such separate abolition statute was located or is cited here. Many other states retain fault-based grounds for divorce alongside or instead of no-fault grounds; that comparison is not independently verified here.

RESIDENCY REQUIREMENT FOR FILING (AND THE SAME-SEX MARRIAGE EXCEPTION)
Except as provided by a specific statutory exception, a judgment of dissolution of marriage may not be entered in California unless one of the parties has been a resident of California for six months and a resident of the county in which the proceeding is filed for three months, both periods measured immediately preceding the filing of the petition. A distinct statutory exception allows a judgment of dissolution, nullity, or legal separation of a marriage between persons of the same sex to be entered even if neither spouse is a California resident or domiciliary at the time of filing, if the marriage was entered into in California and neither party resides in a jurisdiction that will dissolve the marriage — with a rebuttable presumption that a jurisdiction not recognizing the marriage will not dissolve it. In that circumstance, the superior court in the California county where the marriage was entered is the proper court for the proceeding, and the case is adjudicated under California law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b), a judgment of dissolution of marriage may not be entered unless one of the parties to the marriage has been a resident of this state for six months and of the county in which the proceeding is filed for three months next preceding the filing of the petition."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2320(a) (California Legislative Information text), the six-month state / three-month county residency requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2320.)
  "(b) (1) A judgment for dissolution, nullity, or legal separation of a marriage between persons of the same sex may be entered, even if neither spouse is a resident of, or maintains a domicile in, this state at the time the proceedings are filed, if the following apply: (A) The marriage was entered in California. (B) Neither party to the marriage resides in a jurisdiction that will dissolve the marriage. If the jurisdiction does not recognize the marriage, there shall be a rebuttable presumption that the jurisdiction will not dissolve the marriage. (2) For the purposes of this subdivision, the superior court in the county where the marriage was entered shall be the proper court for the proceeding. The dissolution, nullity, or legal separation shall be adjudicated in accordance with California law."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2320(b)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text), the same-sex-marriage exception to the residency requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2320.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's dissolution-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or divorce. This document is informational: it does not itself dissolve a marriage, establish residency, or determine grounds for any specific case; only a court judgment does that. Two of this clause's citations — § 2320(a) and § 2320(b)(1)-(2) — are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2320); both are quoted because they state two distinct rules (the general six-month/three-month residency requirement and a specific exception to it for same-sex marriages entered in California), not because a second independent source was located for either. Nothing in this clause states, or is evidence of, whether either party to a specific marriage actually satisfies the general residency requirement or the same-sex-marriage exception, or whether any particular county is one where filing would be proper for a specific case.

THE SIX-MONTH WAITING PERIOD BEFORE A JUDGMENT BECOMES FINAL
Subject to a small set of statutory exceptions, no judgment of dissolution becomes final for the purpose of terminating the marriage relationship of the parties until six months have expired, measured from the date of service of a copy of the summons and petition, or the date of the respondent's appearance, whichever occurs first. A court may extend that six-month period for good cause shown.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Subject to subdivision (b) and to Sections 2340 to 2344, inclusive, no judgment of dissolution is final for the purpose of terminating the marriage relationship of the parties until six months have expired from the date of service of a copy of summons and petition or the date of appearance of the respondent, whichever occurs first. (b) The court may extend the six-month period described in subdivision (a) for good cause shown."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2339(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the six-month waiting period and its trigger event (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2339.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's dissolution-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or divorce. This document is informational: it does not itself dissolve a marriage, establish residency, or determine grounds for any specific case; only a court judgment does that. This is a single statutory section (§ 2339, subdivisions (a) and (b)); no additional independent source was found for this. Subdivision (a) itself cross-references a further set of exceptions (Sections 2340 to 2344) that this document's research did not independently fetch or verify, and which are not described here.

PROPERTY DIVISION ABSENT A SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT — THE COMMUNITY-PROPERTY DEFAULT
Absent Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee's written agreement, their oral stipulation in open court, or another statutory exception, a court in a dissolution or legal separation proceeding is required to divide the community estate of the parties equally. Where the parties instead reach and document their own agreement on how to divide property, that agreement — not this default rule — controls the division; the terms such an agreement would contain are addressed by this document's companion Marital Settlement Agreement document and are not restated here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except upon the written agreement of the parties, or on oral stipulation of the parties in open court, or as otherwise provided in this division, in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, the court shall, either in its judgment of dissolution of the marriage, in its judgment of legal separation of the parties, or at a later time if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to make such a property division, divide the community estate of the parties equally."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2550 (California Legislative Information text), the equal-division default rule and its written-agreement exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2550.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's dissolution-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or divorce. This document is informational: it does not itself dissolve a marriage, establish residency, or determine grounds for any specific case; only a court judgment does that. This is a single statutory section (§ 2550); no additional independent source was found for this. This same section is independently cited in this corpus's Marital Settlement Agreement document (clause msa_equal_division_default) for the settlement-terms context; it is cited again here, independently re-verified against the statute's live text, only to state the default a court applies when no settlement exists — this clause does not restate that document's fuller treatment of community versus separate property, the date-of-separation test, or the written-agreement exception's mechanics.

INFORMATION REFERENCED WHEN A DISSOLUTION PETITION IS FILED
A proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation is commenced by filing a petition captioned "In re the Marriage of Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee," which states whether it seeks dissolution or legal separation and sets out, among other matters, the date of marriage and the date of separation. For reference: Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee were married on June 12, 2015 and identify March 1, 2026 as their date of separation, for a proceeding contemplated in Sacramento County. This information sheet gathers that background information; it is not the petition itself and does not commence a court proceeding.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Pat Morgan: ☐ _________________________
